title: Complete AI Fundamentals Professional Certificate
description: A full 20-module program from complete beginner to AI-literate professional: AI & ML fundamentals, generative AI, prompt engineering, AI productivity tools, AI for writing/creativity/business/education/software/automation, AI ethics, AI across industries, data literacy, AI entrepreneurship, 10 practical AI projects, a capstone and a Certificate of Completion.
outcomes: Understand AI, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI
Write effective prompts and use ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Copilot
Apply AI to writing, creativity, business, education and software
Use AI automation, and understand machine learning and data literacy
Apply AI ethically and responsibly across industries
Build practical AI projects and an AI portfolio for your career
about: This is the complete TIH AI Fundamentals Professional Certificate, rebuilt into twenty modules that take you from complete beginner to AI-literate professional.

Every content lesson has a unique educational video and printable notes; downloadable resources cover a Prompt Library, AI Toolkit Guide, Business AI templates and an AI Ethics Checklist. Ten practical AI projects and a capstone build your AI portfolio.

Software & tools: ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, Claude AI, Perplexity, NotebookLM, Canva AI, Adobe Firefly, GitHub Copilot, Google Workspace, Microsoft Office, Zapier, Make and Notion AI. You finish with a portfolio and — after the graduation assessment — a Certificate of Completion.
requirements: No prior experience required — we start from the basics
A device with internet access to use AI tools
A willingness to practise with AI tools and verify their output

faqs.question: Do I need coding skills to use AI tools?
faqs.answer: Absolutely not. ChatGPT, Gemini, and all the tools in this course are designed for everyday users. If you can type, you can use AI effectively.

faqs.question: Are the AI tools covered in this course free?
faqs.answer: ChatGPT and Gemini both offer free tiers that are sufficient for this entire course. We will also cover some premium features available at low cost.

faqs.question: Will AI take my job?
faqs.answer: This course addresses this question directly. The evidence shows AI replaces tasks, not entire jobs, and people who know how to use AI will be far more valuable than those who do not.

faqs.question: Is this course updated for the latest AI tools?
faqs.answer: Yes. TIH updates this course quarterly to reflect the rapidly evolving AI landscape. Enrolled students receive all updates at no extra charge.

🧭 Welcome to the Course

This lesson explains Welcome to the Course so you can understand the course, core AI ideas, career directions, evidence requirements, and the final capstone. You will connect the idea to an AI system, test it, identify risk, and produce a verified answer.

Definition

Welcome to the Course is a core topic in Course Orientation, studied through its purpose, inputs, method, outputs, limitations, risks, and responsible human use.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Welcome to the Course

Welcome to the Course is a core topic in Course Orientation, studied through its purpose, inputs, method, outputs, limitations, risks, and responsible human use.

AI system

a machine-based system that infers from inputs how to generate predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions for explicit or implicit objectives

AI literacy

the knowledge and judgment needed to understand, use, evaluate, and discuss AI responsibly

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Detailed explanation

Welcome to the Course is a core topic in Course Orientation, studied through its purpose, inputs, method, outputs, limitations, risks, and responsible human use. A useful explanation separates the user’s objective, input or data, operational logic, output, affected people, and decision authority. AI does not make evidence, ethics, or responsibility disappear.

  • Purpose: state the exact task, user, value, and boundary.
  • Evidence: understand data, sources, examples, assumptions, and what may be missing.
  • Evaluation: compare output with requirements, a baseline, representative tests, and consequences of error.
  • Governance: assign human responsibility, protect rights and information, document versions, and monitor use.

How the process works

  1. Purpose: define the goal, users, context, required evidence, and unacceptable outcomes.
  2. Inputs: prepare authorized data or context and record source, quality, limits, and assumptions.
  3. AI process: use the model or method within defined permissions and preserve output and version evidence.
  4. Verified outcome: verify, correct, explain limitations, obtain human approval, and monitor the real result.

Worked example

A learner identifies a community or business problem, separates tasks suitable for AI from tasks needing human authority, and plans evidence, safeguards, and a capstone demonstration.

Analysis: this is responsible because the goal is narrow, evidence is visible, important facts are checked, human authority remains, and failure has a response.

Prompt and evaluation laboratory

Reusable prompt: “Help me with [specific task] for [audience and purpose]. Use only [approved context/source]. Requirements: [criteria]. Do not invent missing facts; mark uncertainty and ask for necessary information. Return [format]. I will verify the result against [rubric/source/test].”

Evaluation: Check relevance, factual support, completeness, logic, bias, privacy, rights, safety, accessibility, tone, format, and consistency. Record what was changed and why.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: accepting fluent output as fact. Correction: verify claims with primary sources, calculations, tests, or qualified experts.
  • Mistake: uploading confidential information. Correction: use fictional or authorized minimum data and review current data controls.
  • Mistake: judging from one impressive example. Correction: test representative, difficult, edge, and failure cases against a baseline.
  • Mistake: removing humans from accountability. Correction: define who reviews, decides, overrides, reports harm, and stops the system.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a learner apply Welcome to the Course to a real task responsibly?

Answer: Define the user, decision, desired result, limits, and whether AI is actually appropriate. Gather only authorized, relevant information and document its source, quality, date, gaps, and affected groups. Choose a suitable model or tool from current official information, then save the prompt, settings, version, and output. Compare the result with a non-AI baseline or trusted answer and test ordinary, difficult, edge, and misuse cases. Check factual support, bias, privacy, security, copyright, accessibility, and the cost of mistakes. Correct the work rather than hiding errors, explain uncertainty and exclusions, obtain accountable human approval, offer a fallback or appeal where people may be affected, and monitor real outcomes. If evidence does not show adequate benefit and safety, improve the design or do not use AI.

Summary

Welcome to the Course belongs to Course Orientation. Competence means defining it accurately, connecting inputs to outputs, testing evidence, recognizing limitations, protecting people, and keeping human judgment accountable.

Responsible AI boundary: AI output can be false, biased, unsafe, outdated, or inappropriate. Do not enter secrets or personal data without authorization. Verify important claims with primary sources and qualified people. Keep humans accountable for decisions, especially in health, law, finance, education, employment, public services, and safety.

  • NIST: AI Risk Management Framework

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you understand the course, core AI ideas, career directions, evidence requirements, and the final capstone.   2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.

AreaEvidence of quality

✨ Hands-on Practice

token

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you understand how systems generate text, images, audio, video, and multimodal content, including limits and verification. Begin with a real user need and use public, fictional, or properly authorized data. A polished output without evidence, evaluation, and responsibility is incomplete.

Required deliverables

  1. Problem statement, users, stakeholders, current workflow, exclusions, and baseline.
  2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

Worked project model

A learner asks for a public-event announcement, checks every name, date, quotation, and claim against the approved brief, edits the language, and labels synthetic media when appropriate.

The project compares its AI-assisted result with a simple non-AI baseline and records corrections instead of hiding them.

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.
EvidenceTraceable inputs, representative tests, metrics, error analysis, and reproducible versions.
ResponsibilityPrivacy, fairness, rights, security, human authority, disclosure, fallback, and accountability.
CommunicationUsable prototype, honest limitations, clear documentation, reflection, and next decision.

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. Module 4: Prompt EngineeringApplied AI project

⌨️ Prompt Engineering Project

Prompt Engineering Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Prompt Engineering Project

Prompt Engineering Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

prompt

the input, instruction, context, examples, and constraints supplied to an AI system

few-shot prompting

providing a small number of examples to demonstrate the desired pattern or format

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you write clear instructions, examples, constraints, output formats, and evaluation criteria, then improve results systematically. Begin with a real user need and use public, fictional, or properly authorized data. A polished output without evidence, evaluation, and responsibility is incomplete.

Required deliverables

  1. Problem statement, users, stakeholders, current workflow, exclusions, and baseline.
  2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

A strong prompt states the audience, purpose, source material, exclusions, tone, length, required structure, and verification rule; the learner compares the output with a rubric and revises one variable at a time.

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. 🛠️ Productivity Lab

Productivity Lab is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

feature availability

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you compare AI tools by task fit, evidence, privacy, accessibility, cost, current capability, and export workflow. Begin with a real user need and use public, fictional, or properly authorized data. A polished output without evidence, evaluation, and responsibility is incomplete.

Required deliverables

  1. Problem statement, users, stakeholders, current workflow, exclusions, and baseline.
  2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

Worked project model

The learner tests two tools on the same non-confidential task, records date, model or mode when visible, quality, citations, speed, accessibility, limits, and required corrections instead of declaring a permanent winner.

The project compares its AI-assisted result with a simple non-AI baseline and records corrections instead of hiding them.

Assessment rubric

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.
EvidenceTraceable inputs, representative tests, metrics, error analysis, and reproducible versions.
ResponsibilityPrivacy, fairness, rights, security, human authority, disclosure, fallback, and accountability.

Model conclusion

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. The correct decision may be to improve, limit, postpone, or reject AI when a simpler method is safer or more effective.

Responsible AI boundary: AI output can be false, biased, unsafe, outdated, or inappropriate. Do not enter secrets or personal data without authorization. ✍️ Writing Project

Writing Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Writing Project

Writing Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

authorship

responsibility for creating, reviewing, and standing behind a work

source grounding

constraining or checking output against identifiable reliable evidence

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you use AI to support communication while preserving accuracy, authorship, audience fit, sources, confidentiality, and human voice. Begin with a real user need and use public, fictional, or properly authorized data. A polished output without evidence, evaluation, and responsibility is incomplete.

Required deliverables

  1. Problem statement, users, stakeholders, current workflow, exclusions, and baseline.
  2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

Worked project model

A learner supplies approved facts for a scholarship email, requests a structured draft, checks every factual statement, rewrites for natural voice, removes private information, and approves the final message personally.

The project compares its AI-assisted result with a simple non-AI baseline and records corrections instead of hiding them.

Assessment rubric

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.
EvidenceTraceable inputs, representative tests, metrics, error analysis, and reproducible versions.
ResponsibilityPrivacy, fairness, rights, security, human authority, disclosure, fallback, and accountability.
CommunicationUsable prototype, honest limitations, clear documentation, reflection, and next decision.

Model conclusion

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. The correct decision may be to improve, limit, postpone, or reject AI when a simpler method is safer or more effective.

Module 7: AI for Creativity & DesignApplied AI project

🎨 Creative Project

Creative Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Creative Project

Creative Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

creative brief

a document defining audience, purpose, message, style, format, constraints, deliverables, and approval criteria

provenance

information about the origin, creation history, and modifications of content

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you direct and evaluate AI-assisted visual, audio, video, branding, and presentation work with attention to rights and authenticity. Begin with a real user need and use public, fictional, or properly authorized data. A polished output without evidence, evaluation, and responsibility is incomplete.

Required deliverables

  1. Problem statement, users, stakeholders, current workflow, exclusions, and baseline.
  2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

Worked project model

A designer creates mood-board options from a detailed brief, rejects inaccurate cultural symbols, edits the chosen direction, checks licenses and consent, documents AI assistance, and exports accessible final assets.

The project compares its AI-assisted result with a simple non-AI baseline and records corrections instead of hiding them.

Assessment rubric

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.
EvidenceTraceable inputs, representative tests, metrics, error analysis, and reproducible versions.
ResponsibilityPrivacy, fairness, rights, security, human authority, disclosure, fallback, and accountability.
CommunicationUsable prototype, honest limitations, clear documentation, reflection, and next decision.

Model conclusion

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. The correct decision may be to improve, limit, postpone, or reject AI when a simpler method is safer or more effective.

Responsible AI boundary: AI output can be false, biased, unsafe, outdated, or inappropriate. Do not enter secrets or personal data without authorization. Verify important claims with primary sources and qualified people. Keep humans accountable for decisions, especially in health, law, finance, education, employment, public services, and safety.

training data

examples used to fit or learn a model’s parameters or rules

generalization

a model’s ability to perform usefully on relevant new data rather than only memorizing training examples

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you understand learning types, data splits, training, evaluation, generalization, metrics, and real-world monitoring. Module 9: AI for BusinessApplied AI project

💼 Business AI Project

Business AI Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Business AI Project

Business AI Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

business case

an evidence-based justification comparing need, options, costs, benefits, risks, measures, and recommendation

return on investment

the net benefit of an investment compared with its total cost, interpreted with assumptions and time period

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you connect AI investment to business need, workflow, customers, staff, risk, measurable value, and responsible governance. Begin with a real user need and use public, fictional, or properly authorized data. A polished output without evidence, evaluation, and responsibility is incomplete.

Required deliverables

  1. Problem statement, users, stakeholders, current workflow, exclusions, and baseline.
  2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

A small enterprise pilots AI-assisted customer-message triage, keeps humans responsible for replies, measures response time and correction rate, protects customer data, and expands only if benefits exceed cost and risk.

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. 🎓 Education Project

Education Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Education Project

Education Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

academic integrity

honest learning and research that follows rules for originality, sources, collaboration, and tool use

citation

a reference that identifies the source supporting a claim or borrowed idea

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you use AI to support learning and research without replacing thinking, evidence, attribution, teacher judgment, or academic integrity. Begin with a real user need and use public, fictional, or properly authorized data. A polished output without evidence, evaluation, and responsibility is incomplete.

Required deliverables

  1. Problem statement, users, stakeholders, current workflow, exclusions, and baseline.
  2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

Worked project model

A student attempts a problem first, asks AI for a hint, checks the explanation against course material, writes the answer independently, cites real sources, and discloses AI use according to school policy.

The project compares its AI-assisted result with a simple non-AI baseline and records corrections instead of hiding them.

Assessment rubric

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.
EvidenceTraceable inputs, representative tests, metrics, error analysis, and reproducible versions.
ResponsibilityPrivacy, fairness, rights, security, human authority, disclosure, fallback, and accountability.
CommunicationUsable prototype, honest limitations, clear documentation, reflection, and next decision.

Model conclusion

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. The correct decision may be to improve, limit, postpone, or reject AI when a simpler method is safer or more effective.

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you use AI in software work while preserving requirements, architecture, security, testing, licensing, review, and developer responsibility.   4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.

Module 12: AI AutomationApplied AI project

⚙️ Automation Project

Automation Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Automation Project

Automation Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

automation

use of configured systems to perform repeatable steps with limited manual action

agent

a system that uses a model and tools to pursue a goal across multiple steps within defined permissions and controls

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you design dependable workflows using triggers, actions, conditions, tools, permissions, logs, exceptions, and human approval. Begin with a real user need and use public, fictional, or properly authorized data. A polished output without evidence, evaluation, and responsibility is incomplete.

Required deliverables

  1. Problem statement, users, stakeholders, current workflow, exclusions, and baseline.
  2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

Worked project model

An organization automates intake classification but requires validation, limits tool permissions, logs actions, routes uncertain cases to a person, prevents duplicate execution, and provides rollback and shutdown.

The project compares its AI-assisted result with a simple non-AI baseline and records corrections instead of hiding them.

Assessment rubric

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.
EvidenceTraceable inputs, representative tests, metrics, error analysis, and reproducible versions.
ResponsibilityPrivacy, fairness, rights, security, human authority, disclosure, fallback, and accountability.
CommunicationUsable prototype, honest limitations, clear documentation, reflection, and next decision.

Model conclusion

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. The correct decision may be to improve, limit, postpone, or reject AI when a simpler method is safer or more effective.

⚖️ AI Bias

This lesson explains AI Bias so you can identify and manage fairness, privacy, security, transparency, rights, accountability, and context-specific AI risk. You will connect the idea to an AI system, test it, identify risk, and produce a verified answer.

Definition

AI bias is systematic error or design imbalance that can create inaccurate or unfair outcomes for people or groups.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

AI Bias

AI bias is systematic error or design imbalance that can create inaccurate or unfair outcomes for people or groups.

algorithmic bias

systematic error that can produce unfairly different performance or outcomes across groups

human oversight

meaningful human authority to understand, review, intervene, override, or stop an AI-assisted process

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Detailed explanation

AI bias is systematic error or design imbalance that can create inaccurate or unfair outcomes for people or groups. A useful explanation separates the user’s objective, input or data, operational logic, output, affected people, and decision authority. AI does not make evidence, ethics, or responsibility disappear.

  • Purpose: state the exact task, user, value, and boundary.
  • Evidence: understand data, sources, examples, assumptions, and what may be missing.
  • Evaluation: compare output with requirements, a baseline, representative tests, and consequences of error.
  • Governance: assign human responsibility, protect rights and information, document versions, and monitor use.

How the process works

  1. Map people and harms: define the goal, users, context, required evidence, and unacceptable outcomes.
  2. Measure risk: prepare authorized data or context and record source, quality, limits, and assumptions.
  3. Apply controls: use the model or method within defined permissions and preserve output and version evidence.
  4. Monitor and report: verify, correct, explain limitations, obtain human approval, and monitor the real result.

Worked example

Before using AI to shortlist applicants, an organization tests job relevance and group performance, documents data and limits, offers human review and appeal, monitors outcomes, and remains accountable.

Analysis: this is responsible because the goal is narrow, evidence is visible, important facts are checked, human authority remains, and failure has a response.

Prompt and evaluation laboratory

Evaluation: Check relevance, factual support, completeness, logic, bias, privacy, rights, safety, accessibility, tone, format, and consistency. Record what was changed and why.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: uploading confidential information. Correction: use fictional or authorized minimum data and review current data controls.
  • Mistake: judging from one impressive example. Correction: test representative, difficult, edge, and failure cases against a baseline.
  • Mistake: removing humans from accountability. Correction: define who reviews, decides, overrides, reports harm, and stops the system.

Compare the result with a non-AI baseline or trusted answer and test ordinary, difficult, edge, and misuse cases. Check factual support, bias, privacy, security, copyright, accessibility, and the cost of mistakes. Correct the work rather than hiding errors, explain uncertainty and exclusions, obtain accountable human approval, offer a fallback or appeal where people may be affected, and monitor real outcomes. 📊 Data Project

Data Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Data Project

Data Project is a practical AI assignment that converts a defined user need into a tested, documented, and responsibly governed demonstration.

data quality

the degree to which data are accurate, complete, consistent, timely, valid, representative, and fit for purpose

dataset

an organized collection of observations, records, measurements, labels, or other data

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you collect, clean, describe, visualize, protect, and interpret data so AI decisions rest on fit evidence. Begin with a real user need and use public, fictional, or properly authorized data. A polished output without evidence, evaluation, and responsibility is incomplete.

Required deliverables

  1. Problem statement, users, stakeholders, current workflow, exclusions, and baseline.
  2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

Worked project model

A learner defines a question, documents data source and consent, removes duplicates, treats missing values deliberately, calculates basic summaries, creates an honest chart, and states what the data cannot prove.

The project compares its AI-assisted result with a simple non-AI baseline and records corrections instead of hiding them.

Assessment rubric

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.
EvidenceTraceable inputs, representative tests, metrics, error analysis, and reproducible versions.
ResponsibilityPrivacy, fairness, rights, security, human authority, disclosure, fallback, and accountability.
CommunicationUsable prototype, honest limitations, clear documentation, reflection, and next decision.

Model conclusion

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. The correct decision may be to improve, limit, postpone, or reject AI when a simpler method is safer or more effective.

Responsible AI boundary: AI output can be false, biased, unsafe, outdated, or inappropriate. Do not enter secrets or personal data without authorization.   5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

Worked project model

A project uses public, fictional, or properly authorized data; defines users and exclusions; compares a baseline; tests accuracy, usefulness, bias, privacy, and failure; and documents human responsibility.

The project compares its AI-assisted result with a simple non-AI baseline and records corrections instead of hiding them.

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.
EvidenceTraceable inputs, representative tests, metrics, error analysis, and reproducible versions.
ResponsibilityPrivacy, fairness, rights, security, human authority, disclosure, fallback, and accountability.
CommunicationUsable prototype, honest limitations, clear documentation, reflection, and next decision.

Model conclusion

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. a record of risks, likelihood, impact, owner, controls, status, and review date

success metric

a defined measure with method, baseline or target, time period, and responsible owner

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Project brief

Build a small, testable demonstration that shows how you integrate problem research, solution comparison, workflow design, prototype building, evaluation, documentation, and presentation. Begin with a real user need and use public, fictional, or properly authorized data. A polished output without evidence, evaluation, and responsibility is incomplete.

Required deliverables

  1. Problem statement, users, stakeholders, current workflow, exclusions, and baseline.
  2. Input or data plan covering source, permission, quality, representativeness, privacy, and limitations.
  3. Prompt, model, tool, or automation design with versions, assumptions, permissions, and human checkpoints.
  4. Working prototype or demonstration plus normal, edge, failure, and misuse tests.
  5. Evaluation table covering accuracy, usefulness, consistency, bias, safety, privacy, accessibility, cost, and human effort.
  6. Risk register, responsible owner, safeguards, fallback, documentation, presentation, and improvement plan.

Worked project model

The capstone begins with a real need rather than a fashionable tool, documents stakeholders and alternatives, prototypes safely, evaluates against a baseline, records limitations and risks, and presents a justified recommendation.

The project compares its AI-assisted result with a simple non-AI baseline and records corrections instead of hiding them.

Assessment rubric

AreaEvidence of quality
Need & designClear user, problem, workflow, baseline, requirements, and justified AI role.
EvidenceTraceable inputs, representative tests, metrics, error analysis, and reproducible versions.
ResponsibilityPrivacy, fairness, rights, security, human authority, disclosure, fallback, and accountability.
CommunicationUsable prototype, honest limitations, clear documentation, reflection, and next decision.

Model conclusion

The prototype demonstrates a defined use, but deployment should depend on representative evaluation, user feedback, risk controls, accountable human review, current legal and organizational approval, and ongoing monitoring. The correct decision may be to improve, limit, postpone, or reject AI when a simpler method is safer or more effective.

Responsible AI boundary: AI output can be false, biased, unsafe, outdated, or inappropriate. Do not enter secrets or personal data without authorization. Verify important claims with primary sources and qualified people. Keep humans accountable for decisions, especially in health, law, finance, education, employment, public services, and safety.

Authoritative learning references

  • OECD: Updated definition of an AI system
  • NIST: AI Risk Management Framework
  • UNESCO: Generative AI in education and research
  • Official OpenAI documentation: Prompt engineering

lessons.title: 20.1 Certificate Requirements
lessons.html:
Module 20: Assessments & GraduationComplete AI lesson

🎓 Certificate Requirements

This lesson explains Certificate Requirements so you can verify completion requirements, portfolio evidence, reflection, and responsible next steps. You will connect the idea to an AI system, test it, identify risk, and produce a verified answer.

Definition

Certificate requirements are the published lessons, assessments, projects, conduct, and evidence a learner must complete.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Certificate Requirements

Certificate requirements are the published lessons, assessments, projects, conduct, and evidence a learner must complete.

certificate requirement

a published condition that must be satisfied before course completion is recognized

portfolio review

a structured evaluation of work evidence against stated criteria

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Detailed explanation

Certificate requirements are the published lessons, assessments, projects, conduct, and evidence a learner must complete. A useful explanation separates the user’s objective, input or data, operational logic, output, affected people, and decision authority. AI does not make evidence, ethics, or responsibility disappear.

  • Purpose: state the exact task, user, value, and boundary.
  • Evidence: understand data, sources, examples, assumptions, and what may be missing.
  • Evaluation: compare output with requirements, a baseline, representative tests, and consequences of error.
  • Governance: assign human responsibility, protect rights and information, document versions, and monitor use.

How the process works

  1. Check requirements: define the goal, users, context, required evidence, and unacceptable outcomes.
  2. Organize evidence: prepare authorized data or context and record source, quality, limits, and assumptions.
  3. Reflect honestly: use the model or method within defined permissions and preserve output and version evidence.
  4. Plan next action: verify, correct, explain limitations, obtain human approval, and monitor the real result.

Worked example

The learner checks completion records, removes confidential information, verifies ownership and citations, organizes project evidence, records lessons learned, and builds a specific next-step plan.

Analysis: this is responsible because the goal is narrow, evidence is visible, important facts are checked, human authority remains, and failure has a response.

Prompt and evaluation laboratory

Reusable prompt: “Help me with [specific task] for [audience and purpose]. Use only [approved context/source]. Requirements: [criteria]. Do not invent missing facts; mark uncertainty and ask for necessary information. Return [format]. I will verify the result against [rubric/source/test].”

Evaluation: Check relevance, factual support, completeness, logic, bias, privacy, rights, safety, accessibility, tone, format, and consistency. Record what was changed and why.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: accepting fluent output as fact. Correction: verify claims with primary sources, calculations, tests, or qualified experts.
  • Mistake: uploading confidential information. Correction: use fictional or authorized minimum data and review current data controls.
  • Mistake: judging from one impressive example. Correction: test representative, difficult, edge, and failure cases against a baseline.
  • Mistake: removing humans from accountability. Correction: define who reviews, decides, overrides, reports harm, and stops the system.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a learner apply Certificate Requirements to a real task responsibly?

Answer: Define the user, decision, desired result, limits, and whether AI is actually appropriate. Gather only authorized, relevant information and document its source, quality, date, gaps, and affected groups. Choose a suitable model or tool from current official information, then save the prompt, settings, version, and output. Compare the result with a non-AI baseline or trusted answer and test ordinary, difficult, edge, and misuse cases. Check factual support, bias, privacy, security, copyright, accessibility, and the cost of mistakes. Correct the work rather than hiding errors, explain uncertainty and exclusions, obtain accountable human approval, offer a fallback or appeal where people may be affected, and monitor real outcomes. If evidence does not show adequate benefit and safety, improve the design or do not use AI.

Summary

Certificate Requirements belongs to Assessments & Graduation. Competence means defining it accurately, connecting inputs to outputs, testing evidence, recognizing limitations, protecting people, and keeping human judgment accountable.

Responsible AI boundary: AI output can be false, biased, unsafe, outdated, or inappropriate. Do not enter secrets or personal data without authorization. Verify important claims with primary sources and qualified people. Keep humans accountable for decisions, especially in health, law, finance, education, employment, public services, and safety.

Authoritative learning references

  • OECD: Updated definition of an AI system
  • NIST: AI Risk Management Framework
  • UNESCO: Generative AI in education and research
  • Official OpenAI documentation: Prompt engineering

Certificate of Completion

This completion lesson verifies requirements, organizes evidence, reflects on competence and limitations, and creates a responsible next-step plan.

certificate requirement

a published condition that must be satisfied before course completion is recognized

portfolio review

a structured evaluation of work evidence against stated criteria

verification

checking an output against reliable evidence, requirements, tests, and context before relying on it

Detailed explanation

This completion lesson verifies requirements, organizes evidence, reflects on competence and limitations, and creates a responsible next-step plan. A useful explanation separates the user’s objective, input or data, operational logic, output, affected people, and decision authority. AI does not make evidence, ethics, or responsibility disappear.

  • Purpose: state the exact task, user, value, and boundary.
  • Evidence: understand data, sources, examples, assumptions, and what may be missing.
  • Evaluation: compare output with requirements, a baseline, representative tests, and consequences of error.
  • Governance: assign human responsibility, protect rights and information, document versions, and monitor use.

How the process works

  1. Check requirements: define the goal, users, context, required evidence, and unacceptable outcomes.
  2. Organize evidence: prepare authorized data or context and record source, quality, limits, and assumptions.
  3. Reflect honestly: use the model or method within defined permissions and preserve output and version evidence.
  4. Plan next action: verify, correct, explain limitations, obtain human approval, and monitor the real result.

Worked example

The learner checks completion records, removes confidential information, verifies ownership and citations, organizes project evidence, records lessons learned, and builds a specific next-step plan.

Analysis: this is responsible because the goal is narrow, evidence is visible, important facts are checked, human authority remains, and failure has a response.

Prompt and evaluation laboratory

Reusable prompt: “Help me with [specific task] for [audience and purpose]. Use only [approved context/source]. Requirements: [criteria]. Do not invent missing facts; mark uncertainty and ask for necessary information. Return [format]. I will verify the result against [rubric/source/test].”

Evaluation: Check relevance, factual support, completeness, logic, bias, privacy, rights, safety, accessibility, tone, format, and consistency. Record what was changed and why.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: accepting fluent output as fact. Correction: verify claims with primary sources, calculations, tests, or qualified experts.
  • Mistake: uploading confidential information. Correction: use fictional or authorized minimum data and review current data controls.
  • Mistake: judging from one impressive example. Correction: test representative, difficult, edge, and failure cases against a baseline.
  • Mistake: removing humans from accountability. Correction: define who reviews, decides, overrides, reports harm, and stops the system.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a learner apply Certificate of Completion to a real task responsibly?

Answer: Define the user, decision, desired result, limits, and whether AI is actually appropriate. Gather only authorized, relevant information and document its source, quality, date, gaps, and affected groups. Choose a suitable model or tool from current official information, then save the prompt, settings, version, and output. Compare the result with a non-AI baseline or trusted answer and test ordinary, difficult, edge, and misuse cases. Check factual support, bias, privacy, security, copyright, accessibility, and the cost of mistakes. Correct the work rather than hiding errors, explain uncertainty and exclusions, obtain accountable human approval, offer a fallback or appeal where people may be affected, and monitor real outcomes. If evidence does not show adequate benefit and safety, improve the design or do not use AI.

Summary

Certificate of Completion belongs to Assessments & Graduation. Competence means defining it accurately, connecting inputs to outputs, testing evidence, recognizing limitations, protecting people, and keeping human judgment accountable.

Responsible AI boundary: AI output can be false, biased, unsafe, outdated, or inappropriate. Do not enter secrets or personal data without authorization. Verify important claims with primary sources and qualified people. Keep humans accountable for decisions, especially in health, law, finance, education, employment, public services, and safety.
